lead: A beam fails in bending when the stress at its farthest fibre passes the allowable stress, and in shear when the stress at the neutral axis does. Design runs analysis backwards: you know the bending moment and shear force from the BMD and SFD, you know the allowable stresses, and you must pick a cross-section that satisfies both at once. One number fixes the bending size — the required section modulus Z = M/σ_allow. A second check fixes the shear size. Every rolled joist in a steel table and every timber size in a roof was chosen this way.
prereq: You need: 4.2 for M/I = σ/y, 4.3 for Z = I/y_max, 4.5 for τ = VQ/(Ib), and Unit 3 for the BMD and SFD.

sections.h3: Step one: size the section for bending

blocks.text: The bending moment diagram gives the largest moment in the beam, M_max. A section is safe in bending when the stress at its farthest fibre stays at or below the allowable stress. That turns into a demand on the section modulus.

blocks.where: Z_req is the smallest acceptable section modulus (mm³); M_max is the largest bending moment from the BMD (N·mm); σ_allow is the allowable bending stress (N/mm²).

blocks.text: Units do the work for you. Keep M in N·mm and σ in N/mm² and Z comes out in mm³. A moment of 40 kN·m is 40 × 10⁶ N·mm, not 40. Getting this wrong is the single most common mistake in the exam.

items: Draw the SFD and BMD (Unit 3). Record M_max and V_max and where each occurs.
Pick a trial section whose Z about the actual bending axis is at least Z_req.
Check that section for shear using the correct τ_max formula.
If shear fails, increase the web or the area and repeat. If both pass, accept the size.

blocks.text: For a rolled steel section, pick the lightest one in the table whose Z about the bending axis meets Z_req. For a rectangle Z = bd²/6, so depth buys far more strength than width.

A section that passes bending can still fail in shear. Short deep beams and beams with a heavy load just inside a support are the usual cases. Shear stress is largest at the neutral axis, where bending stress is zero.

blocks.where: V_max is the largest shear force from the SFD (N); A = b × d is the whole rectangular area (mm²); τ_allow is the allowable shear stress (N/mm²). The factor 1.5 comes from the parabolic shear distribution of 4.5.

blocks.text: For other shapes use τ_max = VQ/(Ib) at the neutral axis: a solid circle gives 4V/(3A), a thin tube gives about 2V/A. Using plain V/A for a rectangle understates the peak stress by one third and passes sections that would actually crack.

In a long, lightly loaded beam the shear check usually passes with a huge margin. In a short span carrying a big load it decides the section. Shear is bought with area A = bd, from width or from depth; extra depth helps only in direct proportion to the area it adds, without the squared advantage it gives in bending.

sections.h3: Proportioning a rectangle and beams of uniform strength

blocks.text: For width b and depth d, Z = bd²/6 while area A = bd. Doubling d multiplies Z by four but area only by two; doubling b doubles both. Depth is the cheaper way to buy bending strength, which is why beams are deep and narrow.

A frequent exam proportion is d = 2b. Then Z = b(2b)²/6 = 2b³/3, so b = (3 Z_req/2)^(1/3) and d = 2b. Round both up to practical sizes, then recheck bending and shear on the rounded section — rounding down is never allowed.

A section is balanced when both limits are nearly used up. If τ_max sits far below τ_allow the beam is over-designed in shear, usually shallow, and will deflect too much — deflection is a separate check, see Unit 5.

A beam of uniform strength changes its section along the span so that Z(x) = M(x)/σ_allow at every point. Which profile you get depends on what is held constant. Keep the width constant and let the depth follow the moment: a cantilever under a UDL has M ∝ x², so d ∝ x and the side view is a triangle; a cantilever with an end point load has M ∝ x, so d ∝ √x and the side view is a parabola. Keep the depth constant instead and let the width follow the moment: a cantilever with an end point load is then a triangle in plan, and a simply supported beam under a UDL is parabolic in plan, widest at midspan. It saves material but costs fabrication, so standard rolled sections are never made this way.

figure.caption: The design loop: the bending moment fixes the required section modulus, a section is chosen, the shear check either passes it or sends it back for a bigger size.

spec.title: Design checks
spec.aria: Flowchart: find the maximum bending moment, get the required section modulus, choose a section, check shear stress, and accept the final size; a failed shear check sends you back to choose a bigger section.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 4 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m over its whole length. The allowable bending stress is 160 MPa and the allowable shear stress is 100 MPa. Design a rectangular section with depth twice the width, round up to the next 25 mm, and check the section for bending and shear.
steps: Reactions: R = wL/2 = 20 × 4 / 2 = 40 kN. So V_max = 40 kN at each support.
Maximum moment at midspan: M_max = wL²/8 = 20 × 4² / 8 = 40 kN·m = 40 × 10⁶ N·mm.
Required section modulus: Z_req = M_max / σ_allow = 40 × 10⁶ / 160 = 250,000 mm³.
Round up: b = 75 mm, d = 150 mm. Provided Z = 75 × 150² / 6 = 281,250 mm³, which exceeds 250,000 mm³.
Bending check: σ_max = M_max / Z = 40 × 10⁶ / 281,250 = 142.2 MPa ≤ 160 MPa. Safe.
examples.answer: Use a 75 mm × 150 mm rectangle: σ_max = 142.2 MPa against 160 MPa allowed, and τ_max = 5.33 MPa against 100 MPa allowed.
examples.check:
w, L = 20.0, 4.0
sigma, tau_a = 160.0, 100.0
M = w * L**2 / 8 * 1e6
V = w * L / 2 * 1e3
Z = M / sigma
b = (3 * Z / 2) ** (1/3)
d = 2 * b
print('M =', M, 'N.mm')
print('Z_req =', Z, 'mm3')
print('b =', round(b, 1), 'mm')
print('d =', round(d, 1), 'mm')
b2, d2 = 75.0, 150.0
Zp = b2 * d2**2 / 6
print('Z_provided =', Zp, 'mm3')
print('sigma_max =', round(M / Zp, 1), 'MPa')
print('tau_max =', round(1.5 * V / (b2 * d2), 2), 'MPa')

traps: Skipping the shear check after the bending design. Bending picks the trial size; shear can still reject it.
Using τ = V/A for a rectangle instead of 1.5V/A. That understates the peak stress by a third.
Feeding kN·m straight into Z = M/σ. Convert: 40 kN·m = 40 × 10⁶ N·mm, or your Z is a thousand times too small.
Using Z about the wrong axis. A rectangle bent about its other axis has Z = db²/6, not bd²/6.
Rounding the chosen b and d downwards, or rounding up without rechecking σ and τ on the new size.

quiz.q: Define section modulus and state the bending design condition.
quiz.a: Z = I/y_max, in mm³. The section is safe when σ_max = M/Z ≤ σ_allow, so the required value is Z_req = M_max/σ_allow.

quiz.q: Write the maximum shear stress in a solid rectangular section in terms of V and A.
quiz.a: τ_max = 1.5 V/A, at the neutral axis.

quiz.q: Why is depth more effective than width for the bending strength of a rectangle?
quiz.a: Z = bd²/6 depends on d squared but on b only to the first power, while area bd rises with both. Doubling d gives four times the moment capacity for twice the material; doubling b gives only twice for twice the material.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam of span 3 m carries a UDL of 10 kN/m. Allowable bending stress is 120 MPa. Find Z_req.
A 100 mm × 200 mm rectangular section carries a shear force of 60 kN. Find the maximum shear stress and compare it with an allowable of 3 MPa.
quiz.a: A = 20,000 mm². τ_max = 1.5 × 60,000/20,000 = 4.5 MPa, which exceeds 3 MPa, so the section fails in shear.

quiz.q: A beam passes the bending check but fails the shear check. Give two possible changes and the cost of each.
quiz.a: Increase the area (widen the section or add a web) — costs material and self-weight but directly cuts τ = 1.5V/A. Reduce the span or move the load away from the support by adding a support — cuts V_max itself, but changes the structural layout. Deepening helps only in proportion to the area it adds, since τ = 1.5V/(bd), while the same depth in bending raises Z with d². Widening helps shear and bending only linearly.

quiz.q: Explain a beam of uniform strength and say why standard rolled sections are not made that way.
quiz.a: The section varies along the span so that Z(x) = M(x)/σ_allow everywhere, giving a triangular or parabolic profile. The extreme fibre is at the allowable stress at every section, so no material is carried where the moment cannot use it. Rolling mills produce only straight constant-section shapes, fabrication of a tapered beam costs far more than the material saved, and deflection and stability still need checking.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real design codes replace the single allowable stress with partial safety factors on load and material: IS 800 for steel and IS 456 for concrete both work this way, so the working stress method here is the historical base, not the current rule. Plastic design goes further and uses the full yield capacity of the section, giving a shape factor of 1.5 for a rectangle — the same 1.5 that appears in the shear formula, for an unrelated reason. Software now searches thousands of rolled sections and optimises a whole frame, not one beam. Useful search terms: limit state design, plastic section modulus, shape factor, section classification.
